name: 蕎麦 ろうじな (Soba Roujina)

claims.text: This is a soba specialist whose entire focus is buckwheat noodles. Even though the soba is juwari (100% buckwheat, no wheat binder), the kitchen is small and also fries tempura, which is wheat-battered, so airborne flour and shared surfaces make wheat cross-contact likely. No gluten-free or dedicated allergen-safe preparation is documented. Not celiac-safe.

The standard dipping sauce (tsuyu) is a dashi-based sauce built on bonito (katsuobushi); like most Japanese soba tsuyu it would typically contain soy sauce, which is normally brewed with wheat. There is no documented wheat-free tsuyu. Note that the noodles can also be ordered simply with salt rather than tsuyu, which avoids the soy-sauce element (but not the kitchen-wide wheat cross-contact).

The tsuyu and broths are built on bonito (katsuobushi) dashi, so the default dipping sauce is not vegan. Vegetable dishes and tempura are on the menu, but no dedicated vegan preparation or fish-free dashi is documented, so vegans should confirm directly with the restaurant which items can be made without dashi, fish, or other animal products.

Because the noodles are juwari (100% buckwheat with no wheat binder), the noodle itself contains no added wheat flour, and the option to eat the soba with salt instead of the soy-based tsuyu exists. This does not make it celiac-safe given shared-kitchen wheat from tempura, but diners with milder sensitivities may find it useful to discuss with the chef.

name: 蕎麦酒房 櫟 (Soba Shubou Ichii)

claims.text: This is not a celiac-safe restaurant. The soba is hand-cut in-house at varying buckwheat ratios (a nihachi blend that is roughly 80% buckwheat with 20% wheat flour, a nine-tenths blend, and a 100% juwari), all made on the same equipment in the same kitchen. Even the juwari (100% buckwheat) soba shares milling, work surfaces, boiling water, and flour handling with wheat-containing soba, so it cannot be treated as gluten-free.
Soba is boiled in shared water and the menu centers on wheat-containing dishes; cross-contamination is effectively unavoidable. Celiac diners should avoid.

The soba tsuyu and dashi are central to the menu and, like most Japanese soy-sauce-based broths, almost certainly contain wheat. No wheat-free soy sauce or tsuyu is advertised. Treat the dipping sauce and broths as containing wheat.

This is not a vegan-friendly menu. The dashi and broths are bonito- and duck-based, and signature dishes are built around Kawachi duck. No vegan options are advertised, and even vegetable dishes are likely prepared with animal-based dashi.

name: 蕎麦屋 にこら (Sobaya Nikora)

claims.text: The noodles themselves are 100% buckwheat (十割蕎麦) with no wheat binder, but the kitchen is built around soba-mae small plates that include tempura and seasoning systems heavy in dashi and soy — meaning shared surfaces, oil, and broths are very likely. The buckwheat noodle alone does not make a meal here gluten-free or celiac-safe.

No source surfaced any mention of a dedicated gluten-free preparation, separate utensils, or celiac accommodation. Celiac and strictly gluten-free diners should treat this as not safe and confirm directly with the staff before relying on any dish.

Soba is served with a soy- and dashi-based dipping sauce (tsuyu), and many soba-mae plates use soy-based seasonings. As with most Japanese kitchens, the soy sauce almost certainly contains wheat, so the tsuyu and seasoned dishes are not wheat-free.

The standard soba dipping broth is dashi-based (fish/bonito) and many small plates feature fish, duck, or bottarga, so most dishes are not vegan as served. No source described a vegan or vegetarian menu; plant-based diners should ask in advance whether a fish-free broth and meat-free plates can be arranged.

The noodles are genuinely 100% buckwheat (十割), hand-milled and hand-cut daily — a real plus for diners avoiding wheat in the noodle itself, provided cross-contact from the wider kitchen is acceptable to them.

This is a Kansai-style dashi oden specialist. The broth and many classic oden items — hanpen and various neri-mono fish cakes, and ganmodoki/hiryozu (fried tofu fritters typically bound with wheat) — are commonly wheat- and/or soy-based, and everything shares one communal simmering pot, so cross-contamination across items is inherent. This is not a celiac-safe environment and a strict-GF diner should not assume safety here.
No gluten-free accommodation, allergen menu, or ingredient disclosure is documented in any available source.

Soy sauce and dashi are central to the seasoning of the oden broth. Most Japanese soy sauce (koikuchi shoyu) is brewed with wheat, so dishes seasoned with it should be assumed to contain wheat unless the kitchen confirms a wheat-free tamari is used — which is not documented here.

The dashi broth is the heart of the dish and is the base in which all items simmer; Japanese dashi is typically made with katsuobushi (bonito) and/or other fish, so even vegetable items like daikon and Kamo eggplant are cooked in a fish-based broth and are not vegan. No vegan or vegetarian options are documented.

Okonomiyaki and yakisoba here are built on a wheat-flour batter (also containing yam) and cooked on a shared teppan griddle alongside other wheat-based dishes, so cross-contact with gluten is effectively unavoidable. This is not celiac-safe.
The signature okonomiyaki is steam-grilled directly on the same griddle used for all dishes; there is no indication of any gluten-free preparation area or accommodation.

Teppanyaki and okonomiyaki here rely on soy- and dashi-based seasonings and sauces. Most Japanese soy sauce and okonomiyaki/yakisoba sauces contain wheat, and dashi may include additional gluten-containing ingredients, so the seasonings add further gluten risk on top of the batter.

The menu centers on pork, squid, and other meat and seafood cooked on a shared griddle, and sauces and dashi are typically animal-derived (bonito/dashi). There is no indication of vegan options, and cross-contact on the single griddle would be unavoidable.

name: 鉄鍋ぎょうざとお酒の店 杏っ子 (Tetsunabe Gyoza to Osake no Mise Anzukko)

claims.text: Not celiac-safe. The house signature is gyoza wrapped in hand-kneaded wheat dough, so wheat is central to the core menu and flour is present throughout the kitchen.
No gluten-free menu, allergen program, or cross-contamination protocol is documented on the restaurant's own page or in any review.

This is a gyoza izakaya; dumplings are typically served with soy-based dipping sauce, and most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat. Assume soy sauce here is not gluten-free unless staff confirm otherwise.
Not vegan-friendly. The restaurant's own page states all gyoza contain pork, and the menu is built on pork, seafood and cheese fillings.

name: 手打ち蕎麦 かね井 (Teuchi Soba Kanei)

claims.text: The signature is 100% buckwheat (jūwari) soba, but it is served with a wheat/soy-based dipping sauce (tsuyu), so the meal as served is not gluten-free and cross-contact is inherent. No gluten-free accommodation is documented, and foreign celiac guests should not assume safety even though the noodles themselves are pure buckwheat.

The dipping sauce is described as strongly soy-sauce-forward (a bold shoyu aroma rather than a light dashi style). Japanese soy sauce typically contains wheat, so the tsuyu is a wheat-containing element.
The sauce and broth are dashi-based and the menu features duck soba, so standard preparations are not vegan; no vegan or vegetarian options are documented.
No allergen accommodation, allergy-handling protocol, or gluten-free/vegan options are documented in available sources. Confirm any allergy needs directly with the shop.
The noodles themselves are self-milled 100% buckwheat with no wheat flour blended into the dough, so the buckwheat base is unusually pure compared with typical blended (nihachi) soba.

name: 手打うどん春日井 (Teuchi Udon Kasugai)

claims.text: Not celiac-safe. The core product is handmade wheat-flour udon, and the menu centers on wheat-based dishes; flour and shared cooking water make cross-contamination effectively unavoidable in a one-person kitchen.
Tempura (shrimp, chicken/kashiwa, assorted) is wheat-battered and deep-fried; no dedicated gluten-free fryer or separate preparation is indicated in any source.

Dishes are served in a dashi broth, and Japanese udon broths and curry udon are typically built on soy sauce (which usually contains wheat) plus bonito/kombu dashi. Treat the broth, curry udon, and any tsuyu as containing wheat and fish.

No vegan or vegetarian options are documented. The broth is a bonito/dashi-based stock, kitsune and agehana udon include egg and aburaage, and there is no indication of plant-based dashi. Vegan diners should confirm directly before visiting.

No allergy protocols, allergen information, or accommodation practices appear in any available source. With a single owner cooking everything to order, ask directly and well in advance about any allergy needs.
